title: Remembering Where a Sound Came From
section: 讲话 / 报道 / 讲座
transcript: People may remember hearing a sound without remembering which direction it came from. A psychology class tested whether that gap grows when attention is divided. Volunteers sat between two hidden speakers and heard familiar sounds such as a key turning or a dog barking. Half of the volunteers simply listened. The others also had to watch a screen and press a button whenever a shape appeared twice in a row. Afterwards, both groups identified most of the sounds correctly, but the group watching the screen made more mistakes about which side a sound came from. That suggests the source of a sound may be easier to lose track of than its identity during a second task. The setup was deliberately simple, so the result does not tell us how people remember sound locations in a busy street.

questions.prompt: What did the class want to investigate?
options: Whether familiar sounds were more pleasant than unfamiliar ones.
Whether dividing attention affected memory for sound direction.
Whether most people heard better on one side.
Whether people could recognise sounds played at a lower volume.
questions.answer: Whether dividing attention affected memory for sound direction.
questions.explanation: 实验想了解注意力被分散后，参与者是否更难记住声音来自哪个方向。

questions.prompt: What did the two groups do about equally well?
options: Remember which side each sound came from.
Notice repeated shapes on the screen.
Remember the exact order of the sounds.
questions.explanation: 两组都能正确辨认大部分声音，区别主要在判断声音来自哪一侧。
